items.title: Nobody called it the Wars of the Roses at the time
items.claim: The wars between Lancaster and York (1455-1487) are remembered for the red and white rose badges. What is the actual history of those symbols?

options.text: Both sides wore rose badges throughout the conflict
The white rose was a Yorkist badge, but the red Lancastrian rose was largely a Tudor-era invention — Henry VII used the union of the roses as propaganda
The roses came from heraldic tradition dating to the Conquest
The name was coined in 1485 by Henry VII himself

items.reveal_title: The Tudor rose was the spin
items.reveal:
Edward IV used a white rose among other badges. The red rose was a minor Lancastrian badge under Henry IV but rarely used during the wars themselves. The 'Tudor rose' (red and white combined) was created after Henry VII married Elizabeth of York in 1486 — the union as legitimising symbol.

The name 'Wars of the Roses' was popularised by Walter Scott's novel 'Anne of Geierstein' (1829). Shakespeare's 'Henry VI Part 1' invented the Temple Garden scene where nobles pluck the rival roses.
items.why: Historical memory is shaped by later spin. The Tudor regime had every reason to dramatise dynastic union; Shakespeare amplified the imagery; Scott named it. Almost none of that was visible in 1460.

items.title: Alexander the Great died at 32 with no clear successor
items.claim: What happened to Alexander's empire after his death in 323 BCE?

options.text: It passed peacefully to his infant son

Alexander died in Babylon on 10 or 11 June 323 BCE aged 32; his generals (the Diadochi) fought 40 years of wars (323-281 BCE) carving the empire into Hellenistic kingdoms — Ptolemaic Egypt, Seleucid Asia, Antigonid Macedon
It dissolved into independent Greek city-states again

items.reveal:
Alexander had conquered from Macedonia to the Indus in 13 years. Asked on his deathbed who should succeed him, he reportedly said 'to the strongest' (some sources say 'Krateros'). His half-brother Philip III Arrhidaeus (mentally disabled) and posthumous son Alexander IV were both murdered within years.

The Wars of the Diadochi — Antigonus, Ptolemy, Seleucus, Lysimachus, Cassander — produced the Hellenistic world that lasted until Rome absorbed it (Macedon 146 BCE, the Seleucid rump 64 BCE, Ptolemaic Egypt 30 BCE).

The Hellenistic kingdoms spread Greek language and culture across western Asia and Egypt — the koine Greek of the New Testament is a downstream consequence.
items.why: Empires built by single conquerors rarely outlast them. Alexander's death at 32 is one of the great 'what ifs' — but his empire's fracture is also a structural fact about charismatic rule without institutional succession.
